name: Context Rot (Chroma research)
publisher: Chroma (Chroma Research team: Kelly Hong, Anton Troynikov, Jeff Huber)
date_published: July 2025 (technical report and GitHub reproduction toolkit published together)
source_type: vendor blog / technical report (vendor-published empirical benchmark)
claim_value: Tested 18 frontier LLMs (including GPT-4.1, Claude Opus/Sonnet 4 family, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3) across three experiment families (NIAH extension with semantic/distractor variants, LongMemEval conversational QA, and a Repeated Words replication task). Every model's accuracy degrades as input length grows, not only near the stated context limit: degradation is visible from the shortest increments tested and is non-uniform, with some models showing large drops by roughly 113K tokens (about one-tenth of a 1M-token window) and measurable rot even around 50K tokens on models advertising much larger windows.
claim_definition: A benchmark result: controlled experiments varying input length while holding task difficulty constant, measuring retrieval/replication accuracy as a function of token count. It is a direct empirical measurement, not a survey, anecdote, or taxonomy.
reproducibility: Code and data are public: MIT-licensed GitHub repo chroma-core/context-rot ships all three experiment families with scripts to rerun against a reader's own API keys, so reproduction is self-serve rather than requiring Chroma's cooperation. As of this research pass, independent third-party replication (a separate lab or paper rerunning the exact experiments and publishing results) was not found; secondary coverage (ZenML, Adaline Labs, Tinyfish, MorphLLM, Cobus Greyling's newsletter) summarizes and extends the framing but does not constitute independent empirical replication. [uncertain]
publisher_sells_relevant_product: Yes. Chroma is a vector/embedding database vendor. A finding that 'more context is harmful, not just costly' directly supports the case for retrieval-based context curation (Chroma's product category) over naive long-context stuffing, which is a textbook vendor-interest alignment.
conflict_notes: No specific numeric discrepancy was found between the primary report and secondary citations in this pass (unlike the DataHub 82%/83% case flagged elsewhere in this research set). Secondary blog posts (e.g. Tinyfish, MorphLLM) paraphrase the 113K/50K figures consistently with the primary report's own repo and landing page (research.trychroma.com/context-rot), but this pass did not line-by-line diff every secondary citation against the full PDF report. [uncertain]
relationship: Supports the context-engineering framing, but as a technical justification rather than a referendum on prompting: the finding is that longer context is unreliable per se, which argues for curating/compressing what goes into context (context engineering) rather than for abandoning precise prompting. It does not claim prompt wording is unimportant; it is compatible with the counterpoint already logged in article_ideas.md that a prompt is still required to say what you want retrieved or kept.
derivative_of: Explicitly extends the needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH) retrieval-testing tradition and is positioned by Chroma as going beyond simple NIAH by adding semantic (non-literal) matches, distractors, and a conversational-memory task (LongMemEval); it treats 'Lost in the Middle' (Liu et al. 2023) as part of the same lineage of positional/length-sensitivity findings it builds on.
register: practitioner/engineer primarily, with enterprise-IT-buyer secondary appeal (the report is framed as actionable guidance for teams deciding how much context to feed production LLM systems); it is not written or peer-reviewed as an academic paper.
notes: Primary report, landing page, and GitHub repo were all located and cross-checked for consistency on authorship, date, and headline figures; no conflicting figures were found across these primary-adjacent sources in this pass. Independent academic replication status remains unverified (see reproducibility). [uncertain]
already_cited: No. Neither 'Context Rot' nor Chroma is named in article_ideas.md's 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' entry (2026-09-27) or its cited 82%-of-leaders survey figure; that entry cites a different, unnamed 2026 industry report. This Chroma report would be a new citation if added.
new_angle: Adds a concrete, vendor-produced empirical mechanism (degradation starts well before the stated context limit, not just at it) that the existing article_ideas.md entry lacks: that entry currently rests on an opinion survey (82% of leaders agreeing prompts alone don't suffice), not a benchmark. Pulling in Context Rot would let the thought argue 'context engineering has a real technical basis' while the commercial-interest angle (vector-DB vendor benefiting from the problem it diagnoses) gives the counterpoint sharper teeth: the existing entry's point that 'a prompt is still required to state what you want' could be extended to 'and so is judgement about whether this vendor's framing of the fix serves the vendor.'
